As of **December 31, 2023**, Boeing’s filing gives these shares of employees represented:

- **21%** — International Association of Machinists and Aerospace Workers (**IAM**)
- **10%** — Society of Professional Engineering Employees in Aerospace (**SPEEA**)
- **1%** — United Automobile, Aerospace and Agricultural Implement Workers of America (**UAW**)

The filing also says approximately **57,000 employees** were union members.

Compared with fiscal 2023, currency weakness had an unfavorable effect on:

- **Net sales** in **Greater China**, where the renminbi was weak against the U.S. dollar; **Japan**, where the yen was weak; and **Rest of Asia Pacific**, where foreign currencies had a net unfavorable impact.
- **Products gross margin and Products gross margin percentage**. Both increased in fiscal 2024, but foreign-currency weakness partly offset those increases.

The filing identifies these effects in its fiscal 2024 results discussion (Form 10-K pp. 22–24).

Boeing’s 2025 Form 10-K gives four such percentages:

- **46%** of Boeing’s **total revenue** came from non-U.S. customers, including Foreign Military Sales through the U.S. government (p. 10).
- **60%** of **Commercial Airplanes revenue from customer contracts** came from non-U.S. customers (p. 10).
- **Approximately 85%** of **Commercial Airplanes’ total backlog, by dollar value**, was with non-U.S. airlines (p. 33).
- **26%** of **Defense, Space & Security backlog** was attributable to non-U.S. customers (p. 38).

Apple’s fiscal 2025 Form 10-K gives these percentages:

| Percentage | What it measures |
|---|---|
| **40%** | Fiscal 2025 net sales through **direct** distribution channels, as a share of total net sales. |
| **60%** | Fiscal 2025 net sales through **indirect** distribution channels, as a share of total net sales. |
| **12%** | The share of **trade receivables** at September 27, 2025 represented by one customer. |
| **34%** | The share of **trade receivables** at September 27, 2025 represented by third-party cellular network carriers. |
| **46% and 23%** | The shares of **vendor non-trade receivables** at September 27, 2025 represented by each of two individual vendors. |

The two vendor percentages refer to separate vendors, not their combined share. Vendor non-trade receivables arise from component sales to manufacturing vendors; Apple says those sales are not recorded as product net sales. (Form 10-K, pp. 2, 39.)

The filing identifies these developments in calendar 2025:

- **April 23, 2025 — EU Digital Markets Act proceedings:** The European Commission fined Apple **€500 million** in its investigation of App Store steering rules and ordered it to remove restrictions on developers directing users to alternatives outside the App Store. Apple appealed. On the same day, the Commission issued **preliminary findings** in a separate investigation of Apple’s contractual requirements for third-party app developers and marketplaces.
- **April 30, 2025 — Epic Games litigation:** A federal district court found Apple in violation of the 2021 injunction. It barred Apple from charging fees on certain out-of-app purchases or restricting how developers direct customers to them, denied Apple’s request to narrow or vacate the injunction, and referred the matter for consideration of possible criminal-contempt proceedings. Apple appealed.
- **September 2, 2025 — Google antitrust case:** In the case concerning Google’s search arrangements, the D.C. district court ordered remedies after finding Google had violated U.S. antitrust law. The filing notes that the remedies remained subject to further proceedings and appeal.
- **October 2025 — Epic appeal:** The Ninth Circuit heard oral argument on an expedited basis in Apple’s appeal.

*Source: Apple fiscal 2025 Form 10-K, Item 3, “Legal Proceedings” (filing p. 18); legal and regulatory risk discussion (filing p. 14).*

The filing reports these percentages of each segment’s 2022 revenue as recognized on fixed-price contracts:

- **Commercial Airplanes (BCA): 100%**
- **Defense, Space & Security (BDS): 60%**
- **Global Services (BGS): 88%**

These are segment-specific percentages, not percentages of Boeing’s consolidated revenue. *(Form 10-K, printed pp. 111–112)*

The filing gives these figures and dates:

| Item | Filing detail | What it refers to |
|---|---|---|
| **Employees represented** | Approximately **3,200** | IAM District 837 employees at Boeing’s St. Louis-area sites—not the total Boeing workforce. |
| **Strike duration** | **101 days** | The 2025 work stoppage by those employees. |
| **Strike dates** | Began **August 4, 2025**; ended after members voted to ratify a new contract on **November 13, 2025** | The filing says the ratification ended the work stoppage. |
| **Current agreement’s expiration** | **July 2030** | The expiration listed for Boeing’s IAM District 837 agreement in Missouri, as of December 31, 2025. |

The 10-K identifies the approximate employee count, strike duration and contract expiration in its Human Capital disclosure (p. 4); it gives the strike start and ratification dates in its MD&A overview (p. 26). It lists the agreement’s expiration month and year, but does not specify an exact expiration day or the agreement’s start date.

At **January 25, 2026**, NVIDIA reported **$20.8 billion** of goodwill in total:

- **$20.5 billion** was allocated to the **Compute & Networking** reporting unit.
- **$370 million** was allocated to **Graphics**.

Goodwill **increased by $15.6 billion during fiscal 2026**, all allocated to Compute & Networking. The filing separately explains that **$14.4 billion** of this was recorded in connection with NVIDIA’s Groq technology license and hiring of certain Groq employees. It primarily represented the workforce and future development of the licensed technology; the filing says it was tax deductible. **The $14.4 billion is part of—not additional to—the fiscal-year increase.**

*Source: NVIDIA fiscal 2026 Form 10-K, Notes 2 and 5, pp. 61 and 63.*

For fiscal 2024, NVIDIA reported:

- **$774 million** of inventory provision in cost of revenue, for inventory write-downs—including excess or obsolete inventory.
- **Approximately $1.4 billion** of expense in cost of revenue for inventory purchase obligations above current demand projections. The filing says these expenses included supplier charges and penalties for cancellations and underutilization.
- **$2.2 billion total** in provisions for inventory and excess inventory purchase obligations, as reported in the MD&A. The two separately disclosed amounts sum to approximately $2.174 billion, consistent with that rounded total.
- **$540 million of provision releases**, from sales of inventory that had previously been reserved or settlements of excess inventory purchase obligations. NVIDIA does not split that release between those two sources.

These amounts are charges and releases recognized during the year, not year-end outstanding balances. (Form 10-K, pp. 40, 68, 70.)

The filing gives these dividend-related amounts in its non-exhibit text:

- **Up to $345 million per year** — Boeing’s estimate of the cash it might need for preferred-stock dividends through the October 15, 2027 mandatory conversion date (printed p. 17).
- **$72 million, or $12.50 per preferred share** — dividends declared in December 2024 for holders of record January 1, 2025; Boeing says it paid them in cash on January 15, 2025 (printed p. 106). The $72 million declaration is also shown in the statement of equity (printed p. 58).
- **$58 million** — preferred dividends accumulated during 2024, deducted in the statement of operations in arriving at net loss attributable to Boeing common shareholders (printed p. 54).

These are different measures: the $345 million is an annual cash-requirement estimate; the $72 million is a declared dividend; and the $58 million is the amount accumulated during 2024 for the reported earnings-per-share calculation.

Amounts are in **millions**. Excluding unrealized gains on securities still held at fiscal year-end:

- **Publicly held equity securities:** **$88 million net realized gain** on securities sold. The filing says this is the difference between sale proceeds and the securities’ carrying value at the start of the period—or purchase date, if later.
- **Non-marketable equity securities:** **$816 million in unrealized gains** and **$59 million in impairments and unrealized losses**, for a **net gain of $757 million**. The filing says gains and losses on these investments are recognized in “Other income (expense), net.”
  - A **$565 million unrealized gain** resulted from a private-company investment’s secondary equity transaction in the fourth quarter. It is included in—not additional to—the $816 million.

Together, the disclosed fiscal 2025 amounts above imply a **net gain of $845 million** ($88 million + $816 million − $59 million). This excludes the **$163 million** of unrealized gains on publicly held securities held at year-end. (Form 10-K, pp. 66, 68–69.)

NVIDIA said the Ukraine war and the sanctions and export controls imposed in response had these business effects:

- They **blocked the passage of NVIDIA products, services, and support into Russia, Belarus, and certain regions of Ukraine**.
- In fiscal 2023, NVIDIA **stopped direct sales to Russia** and later **closed its Russian business operations**. The filing says direct sales to Russia in fiscal 2022 had been immaterial.
- The war **had affected end-customer sales in EMEA**.
- NVIDIA’s revenue from **partners that sold into Russia may have been negatively affected**.

The filing says the EMEA sales impact might continue in the future; I have not included effects it describes only as future risks. (Form 10-K, pp. 28, 37)

The filing identifies two operating businesses with 2024 affiliate borrowings:

| Business | 2024 affiliate borrowing amounts |
|---|---|
| **Clayton Homes** | Borrowings from Berkshire finance affiliates **increased by $6.6 billion** during 2024, reaching **$24.3 billion** at December 31, 2024. |
| **Pilot Travel Centers** | Borrowed **$5.7 billion** from Berkshire insurance subsidiaries in March 2024 and repaid **$1.0 billion** during the year. That implies about **$4.7 billion** remained outstanding at year-end; the filing does not state that ending balance directly. |

Amounts are rounded to the nearest $0.1 billion. The Clayton figures appear in the manufacturing discussion (K-48); the Pilot figures appear in the Pilot discussion and borrowing note (K-53 and K-99).

The filing gives both an **overall estimate** and **year-by-year costs incurred**:

- **“approximately $700 million”** — Pfizer’s expected costs **in connection with separating Upjohn**. The filing says **“approximately 75%”** had been incurred **“since inception and through December 31, 2021.”** It says these charges include costs and expenses related to **separation of legal entities and transaction costs**. (MD&A, printed p. 26)
- **“$434 million in 2020”** and **“$83 million in 2019”** — separation-related costs Pfizer says it incurred in those years, included in **Discontinued operations––net of tax**. These primarily related to professional fees for regulatory filings and separation activities in finance, tax, legal and information-system functions, as well as investment-banking fees. (Note 2B, printed p. 65)

The filing gives the first figures as an approximate total and progress estimate, and the latter as costs incurred in specific years.

Pfizer’s 2024 Form 10-K gives these Haleon ownership figures:

- **32%** as of **December 31, 2023**.
- **Approximately 23%** after the **March 2024 sale**; the filing also refers to Pfizer’s ownership having fallen from about 32% to about 23% when calculating its share of a dividend with a first-quarter 2024 record date.
- **Approximately 15%** after the **October 2024 sale**, and as of **December 31, 2024**.
- **Approximately 7%** after Pfizer sold another portion of its investment in the **first quarter of 2025**.

The filing discusses the 32%, 23% and 15% figures in Note 2C, and the later reduction to about 7% in MD&A. (Form 10-K pp. 47, 66.)

The Form 10-K reports these adoption effects, in **millions of dollars**:

| Scope | Amount | What it measures |
|---|---:|---|
| **Firm — allowance for credit losses** | **−$587** | Net decrease from adoption on January 1, 2023, under the modified-retrospective method. |
| **Firm — allowance for loan losses by portfolio** | **−$489** consumer excluding credit card; **−$100** credit card; **+$2** wholesale | The portfolio components of the allowance-for-loan-losses adjustment. Together, they net to the Firm’s **−$587**. |
| **Consumer & Community Banking (CCB) — allowance for loan losses** | **−$591** | A separately reported CCB adoption impact, described as driven by residential real estate and credit card. |
| **Firm — retained earnings** | **+$446** | Increase in retained earnings **after tax** from adoption. |

The CCB figure is disclosed separately from the Firm-wide allowance figures; the report does not explain the difference between the CCB amount and the Firm’s portfolio breakdown. (2023 Form 10-K, printed pp. 70, 132, 159, 173.)

As of **January 31, 2022**, the filing gives these counts:

- **Walmart U.S.**: **approximately 4,600 pickup locations** and **more than 3,500 same-day delivery locations**.
- **Walmart International**: **approximately 2,900 pickup locations** and **over 1,900 delivery locations**.

The U.S. figures are for its pickup and same-day delivery services; the International figures are for pickup and delivery services, without a same-day qualifier on the delivery count. (Form 10-K, pp. 7, 9.)

The filing reports **two related fiscal 2025 repayment figures**:

- **$3,468 million** — “Repayments of long-term debt” in the long-term-debt balance rollforward. (MD&A, p. 44)
- **$3,373 million** — total repayment of matured debt in Note 6’s table of significant long-term debt repayments. The table itemizes it as:
  - **$1,500 million** — April 22, 2024 maturity
  - **$990 million** — July 8, 2024 maturity
  - **$253 million** — July 18, 2024 maturity, denominated in yen
  - **$630 million** — December 15, 2024 maturity  
  (Note 6, p. 69)

The **$3,373 million** is the total of those specified matured-debt repayments; it is distinct from the **$3,468 million** rollforward figure.

The 10-K gives three annual capacity figures for Huizhou, all in **millions of metric tons per year**:

- **Ethylene: 1.6**
- **Polyethylene: 1.7**
- **Polypropylene: 0.9**

These are Huizhou’s listed capacities in the corresponding product categories. The table identifies the complex as **100% ExxonMobil interest**. (Form 10-K, p. 23)

The filing identifies these **PTC-related balances at December 31, 2023** (amounts in U.S. dollars):

| Balance | Amount |
|---|---:|
| PTC reportable-segment identifiable assets | **$21.404 billion** |
| PTC goodwill | **$6.605 billion** |
| PTC and subsidiaries’ notes payable and other borrowings | **$5.776 billion** |
| Other intangible assets, net, explicitly attributed to PTC | **approximately $6.6 billion** |
| Receivables of railroad, utilities and energy businesses explicitly related to PTC | **approximately $2.1 billion** |
| Inventories, materials and supplies attributable to PTC | **approximately $1.7 billion** |

The segment table reports identifiable assets and goodwill separately. The other amounts are portions of consolidated balances that the filing specifically attributes to PTC. I’ve excluded annual revenues, expenses and other flows, as well as acquisition-date values. *(Form 10-K, pp. K-88–K-91, K-102, K-113–K-114.)*

The 2021 Form 10-K identifies these projects:

- **Bacalhau Phase 1** in Brazil — funded in 2021 and reached final investment decision in June.
- **North Field Production Sustainment Integrated Drilling and Looping** in Qatar — funded in 2021.
- **Jansz-Io Compression** in Australia — funded in 2021.
- **Huizhou chemical complex** in China — reached final investment decision in 2021.

Sources: Form 10-K pp. 18–20, 46, and 53.

As of January 31, 2026, Walmart reports these amounts for its receive-fixed-rate, pay-fixed-rate cross-currency swaps designated as cash-flow hedges:

- **$6,020 million** — notional amount.
- **$(920) million** — fair value, meaning the swaps were in a **$920 million liability position**. The filing says this was primarily classified in “deferred income taxes and other” on the balance sheet.

The market-risk discussion also describes that fair value, rounded, as a **$0.9 billion liability**. Sources: Note 7, p. 69; Item 7A, p. 47.

The 10-K names these lapped fiscal 2023 items as contributors to fiscal 2024 improvements:

| Fiscal 2024 result | Lapped item named |
|---|---|
| **Consolidated gross profit rate** increased 27 basis points; the filing says the increase was driven mainly by Walmart U.S. | Higher markdowns in the prior year. The Walmart U.S. segment’s gross profit rate rose 20 basis points for the same reason—lapping higher **net** markdowns. |
| **Sam’s Club gross profit rate** increased 55 basis points. | Elevated markdowns in the prior year. |
| **Consolidated operating expenses as a percentage of net sales** decreased 60 basis points. | $3.3 billion in opioid-related legal-settlement charges and $0.8 billion in Walmart International reorganization and restructuring charges. |
| **Walmart International operating expenses as a percentage of segment net sales** decreased 152 basis points. | Business reorganization and restructuring charges related to Flipkart and Massmart. |
| **Return on investment (ROI)** increased to 15.0% from 12.7%. | Opioid-related legal-settlement charges and reorganization and restructuring expenses, all recorded in fiscal 2023. |

The filing also says consolidated operating margin increased 83 basis points due to the factors described above. I’ve treated repeated discussions of the same result—such as the consolidated gross-profit-rate discussion—as one result. (MD&A, pp. 38, 41–44.)

The 2024 Form 10-K gives these figures for Pioneer:

- **Share of ExxonMobil at year-end 2024:** Pioneer represented **19% of consolidated assets** and **4% of consolidated revenues**. (Management’s internal-control report, p. 75.)
- **Contribution to 2024 reported results:** From the May 3 acquisition through December 31, Pioneer contributed **$17.008 billion in sales and other operating revenues** and **$1.710 billion in net income attributable to ExxonMobil**. (Note 21, p. 121.)
- **Proved reserves added:** The acquisition added **2.3 billion oil-equivalent barrels** of proved reserves. (Oil and Gas Reserves, p. 127.)

The $17.008 billion and $1.710 billion figures are for Pioneer’s post-acquisition period, not a full year. The report also says Permian production averaged about **1.185 million oil-equivalent barrels per day** in 2024, around **570,000 barrels per day above the prior year**; that is ExxonMobil’s total Permian production and increase, not a Pioneer-only figure. (MD&A, p. 49.)

ExxonMobil gives four quantified sensitivities:

| Change | Stated annual effect |
|---|---|
| **Brent crude: $1/barrel** | Approximately **$700 million** on 2026 Upstream earnings, after tax |
| **Henry Hub gas: $0.10/MMBtu** | Approximately **$90 million** on 2026 Upstream earnings, after tax |
| **TTF gas: $0.10/MMBtu** | Approximately **$20 million** on 2026 Upstream earnings, after tax |
| **Expected long-term return on pension assets: 0.5 percentage-point decrease worldwide** | Approximately **$150 million increase** in annual pension expense, before tax |

For the three market-price sensitivities, an increase or decrease in the benchmark price has a corresponding favorable or adverse effect. They apply to Upstream consolidated plus equity-company earnings and exclude derivatives. The Brent sensitivity includes oil-linked LNG sales. (Market Risks, report p. 62; Pension Benefits, report p. 67.)

The filing attributes the charges to the severe initial effects of COVID-19 on commercial airlines and aircraft manufacturers, which were especially important to PCC. In its second-quarter 2020 reassessment, Berkshire considered airlines’ announcements about potential future demand, employment levels and aircraft orders; manufacturers’ announced production cuts; and actions Berkshire was taking or might take to restructure operations.

Given those conditions, Berkshire judged it prudent to raise the discount rates and lower its previous long-term cash-flow forecasts used in the impairment reviews. Those revised assumptions led to the goodwill and indefinite-lived intangible-asset impairment charges. Nearly all of the approximately $10 billion in charges related to PCC, whose goodwill and indefinite-lived intangible assets had largely been recorded when Berkshire acquired it in 2016.

The filing attributes quarter-to-quarter differences in net sales to:

- **Seasonality:** Apple has historically had higher first-quarter sales, partly because of holiday demand.
- **Product and service introductions:** Launches can affect sales. Their timing can change sales to indirect distributors as channels stock new products and reduce older-product inventory; sales can also shift when consumers or distributors anticipate a launch.
- **Demand changes:** Apple generates a significant share of sales from one product, so a decline in demand for it can materially affect quarterly sales. Demand for other products or services may also be lower than expected.
- **Disruptions:** Problems with new launches, IT systems or networks, or logistics, component-supply, or manufacturing partners can affect sales.

These are the filing’s sales-related factors, excluding its separate discussion of gross-margin volatility and downward pressure. (Form 10-K, pp. 7, 18; printed pages 4, 15.)

The filing says these securities are investments in private companies with no readily determinable fair values. NVIDIA therefore uses the measurement alternative: it carries them at cost, less any impairment, and adjusts their value for observable price changes in orderly transactions involving similar investments in the same issuer. Those adjustments can require unobservable inputs, including volatility, expected time to liquidity, the risk-free rate, and rights and obligations specific to the security.

Judgment is also required because NVIDIA assesses impairment quarterly using qualitative and quantitative factors, including the investee’s operating performance and market trends. (Form 10-K, pp. 38, 66–67.)

Lower consumer net charge-offs reflected elevated consumer cash balances, which reduced credit-card charge-offs and increased recoveries; higher vehicle collateral values, which reduced scored-auto charge-offs; and improved home prices and low-rate-driven prepayments, which increased residential mortgage recoveries and reversals of prior write-downs. The filing also says consumer credit performance benefited from improvement in the macroeconomic environment.

The filing attributes PCC’s 11.6% revenue decline to the pandemic’s impact on commercial aviation. Reduced air travel led aircraft manufacturers to cut production, while airlines delayed or canceled orders and the industry reduced inventories. PCC says these lower aircraft production levels hurt revenue in both 2020 and 2021. It also identifies production delays in Boeing’s 737 MAX and 787 programs as an additional adverse factor for PCC over the period.

More broadly, the filing says the sharp drop in production affected PCC’s operations: lower output brought restructuring costs and inefficiencies. PCC’s 2021 pretax earnings nevertheless rose from 2020, reflecting management’s actions to resize and restructure operations, prepare for more normalized demand, and reduced restructuring costs. (Form 10-K, printed pp. K-12 and K-49.)

Pfizer attributed the increase mainly to IPR&D acquired in its 2022 acquisitions of Arena, GBT and Biohaven. It recorded $5.0 billion of IPR&D from Arena, $3.0 billion from GBT and $450 million from Biohaven.

Partly offsetting that growth was a $200 million impairment of an IPR&D asset acquired with Array. The asset related to an unapproved treatment for symptomatic dilated cardiomyopathy associated with a lamin A/C gene mutation; Pfizer said the Phase 3 trial reached futility at a planned interim analysis. (2022 Form 10-K, Notes 2A, 4 and 10.)

The filing attributes the fiscal 2025 increases to:

- **Walmart overall** (up 36 basis points): higher variable pay because performance exceeded plan, increased marketing, and higher depreciation expenses (p. 39).
- **Walmart U.S.** (up 44 basis points): increased marketing, higher variable pay from exceeding planned performance, and increased depreciation (p. 40).
- **Sam’s Club U.S.** (up 44 basis points): higher compensation-related expenses—including associate wage investments and higher variable pay from exceeding planned performance—and elevated technology spending (p. 42).

**Walmart International’s ratio decreased**, so the filing does not identify a fiscal 2025 increase for that segment (p. 41).

Growth in balances in new and existing client accounts, reflecting higher-yielding product offerings, and the timing impact of First Republic deposits transferred to AWM from CCB in the fourth quarter of 2023.

Credit card loan growth, reflecting new accounts and revolving balances; higher wholesale commercial-and-industrial charge-offs, including in Technology, Media & Telecommunications and Healthcare; estimated borrower-fraud losses in certain secured lending facilities; and a charge-off on a client-specific Asset & Wealth Management exposure.

For fiscal 2026, the filing attributes the gross profit rate increases to:

- **Walmart overall:** disciplined inventory management in Walmart U.S. and growth in higher-margin businesses globally.
- **Walmart U.S.:** disciplined inventory management and growth in higher-margin businesses.
- **Sam’s Club U.S.:** operational efficiencies and higher margins in fuel.

Walmart International’s gross profit rate **decreased**, so it is not included. (Form 10-K, pp. 35, 39, 41)

The qualifying figures are:

| Figure | What it represents |
|---|---|
| **$3.2 billion** | Fiscal 2022 proceeds the filing says were **primarily related to new equity funding for Flipkart**. The funding reduced Walmart’s ownership from **approximately 83%** at January 31, 2021, to **approximately 75%**. (pp. 43, 64) |
| **$2.2 billion** | Cash that could be accessed only through dividends or intercompany financing arrangements subject to Flipkart minority-shareholder approval; Walmart expected the cash to be used by Flipkart. (p. 42; also p. 58) |
| **$0.4 billion** | Fiscal 2020 impairment charges in Walmart International, consisting primarily of writing off the carrying value of **Jabong.com**, one of Flipkart’s two fashion trade names. (p. 71) |

The filing also describes Flipkart as majority-owned, but the specific ownership percentages it gives in the qualifying funding passage are **approximately 83% and approximately 75%**. I’ve left out broader company or segment totals that do not specifically tie to Flipkart or one of its businesses.

The filing says growth in the Permian and Guyana was offset mainly by **divestments, the Russia expropriation, and lower production entitlements due to higher prices**. Easing government-mandated curtailments partly countered those reductions. (2022 Form 10-K, p. 52; PDF p. 54.)

ExxonMobil attributes the sharp rise to **demand recovering faster than refining capacity**:

- **Gasoline and diesel demand returned to pre-pandemic levels**; jet-fuel demand was still below historical levels because of continuing COVID-19 effects.
- **Pandemic-era refinery shutdowns and limited investment reduced industry capacity**, tightening the market.
- The company also points to **supply-chain constraints** alongside the demand recovery.

It adds that **increased demand and low inventories**, together with stronger trading and marketing margins, boosted Energy Products’ 2022 earnings. (2022 Form 10-K, pp. 47, 53–54)

Pfizer’s 2023 Form 10-K attributes the roughly **$1.1 billion favorable change** mainly to the swing from **net losses on equity securities in 2022 to net gains in 2023**, and to **lower net interest expense**. Those benefits were partly offset by higher intangible-asset impairment charges.

The equity-securities line improved by about **$2.9 billion**: Pfizer recorded net gains of **$1.590 billion** in 2023, versus net losses of **$1.273 billion** in 2022. The 2023 gains included a **$1.7 billion realized gain on Telavant** and a **$297 million unrealized gain on Cerevel**, partly offset by a **$292 million unrealized loss on BioNTech**. The 2022 losses included **$986 million of unrealized losses** on investments in BioNTech, Allogene and Arvinas.

**Net interest expense fell by $402 million**, from $987 million to $585 million. Interest expense rose by $971 million—from $1.238 billion to $2.209 billion—driven by the **$31 billion of senior notes issued in May 2023 to help finance the Seagen acquisition**. But interest income rose by $1.373 billion, from $251 million to $1.624 billion, as Pfizer invested the net proceeds from that debt issuance; that more than offset the higher expense.

A major counterweight was impairment expense: it rose by **$2.603 billion**, from $421 million to $3.024 billion. The 2023 charges were about $3.0 billion, including impairments for **etrasimod** following changes in development plans and revenue expectations; **Prevnar 13** following updated forecasts and the transition toward higher serotype coverage; and other assets affected by competitive pressures or prioritization decisions.

Other changes also affected the total. Royalty-related income increased by $213 million, and the “other, net” category improved by $624 million; the latter included ViiV and Nimbus dividend income and a **$222 million gain** on the sale of Pfizer’s early-stage rare-disease gene-therapy portfolio to Alexion. These gains were partly offset by lower income from benefit plans, higher legal expenses, and a modest decline in collaboration and out-licensing income. Taken together, the line moved from **$217 million of net deductions in 2022 to $835 million of net income in 2023**. (Form 10-K, MD&A and Note 4.)

Pfizer says the IPR&D gross carrying amount increased mainly because the Metsera acquisition added $8.0 billion of IPR&D. That increase was partly offset by $3.9 billion of impairment charges and transfers of $600 million for Padcev and $590 million for talazoparib (Talzenna) from IPR&D to developed technology rights.

Pfizer says the 2025 intangible-asset impairments were primarily due to changes in development plans and updated long-range commercial forecasts. The $3.9 billion of IPR&D impairments included $1.6 billion for disitamab vedotin, $820 million for Tukysa (tucatinib), and $820 million for osivelotor. The filing gives that overall rationale but does not specify a separate cause for each of those three charges. (2025 Form 10-K, pp. 70, 83.)

Five filings report repurchases of the company’s own common stock under a share repurchase program during fiscal 2025:

| Company | Shares repurchased |
|---|---:|
| NVIDIA | 310 million |
| Apple | 402 million |
| Walmart | 61.9 million |
| JPMorgan Chase | 114.408296 million |
| ExxonMobil | 180.1 million |

The filings report these fiscal-year totals in NVIDIA’s Item 5 (pp. 33–34), Apple’s Note 10 (p. 44), Walmart’s capital-resources discussion (p. 45), JPMorgan Chase’s Item 5 (p. 33), and ExxonMobil’s MD&A (p. 60).

**The other three do not qualify:** Berkshire Hathaway reported no 2025 share repurchases; Pfizer reported none under its publicly announced share-purchase plan; and Boeing’s reported 2025 purchases were employee shares transferred for tax withholding, while its open-market repurchase program had ended in 2020. (Berkshire, K-33 and K-55; Pfizer, p. 89; Boeing, p. 23.)

Three of the eight filings identify the CODM as a group acting collectively:

- **JPMorgan Chase** — The **Operating Committee** acts collectively as the firm’s CODM. *(2024 Form 10-K, p. 70.)*
- **Berkshire Hathaway** — The filing calls the CODM a group comprising the **Chairman and Chief Executive Officer, the Vice Chairman of Insurance Operations, and the Vice Chairman of Non-Insurance Operations**. *(Note 26, p. K-108.)*
